items.headline: A self-replicating npm worm takes over the keyv packages and leaves a session-start hook inside developers' agent configuration
items.diff_narrative: Yesterday carried two security items and both were security sold as a product. Microsoft's Project Perception opened to public preview inside Defender with red, blue and green agent teams handing work between themselves, and Horizon3 raised 250 million dollars above a two-billion valuation on the pitch that offence and defence are now both automated and racing each other. Neither described an incident; both described capability, priced. Today security arrives as the incident, and what got hit is not an enterprise estate but the toolchain a reader would use to build one. An attacker took over the GitHub account of the maintainer behind keyv — a caching library pulled roughly 127 million times a week, which is a download rate and not a count of machines — and drove the repository's own Actions workflow to cut poisoned releases. Aikido counted at least 868 packages across 1,381 versions by early afternoon Central European time and was still counting, with the same maintainer's flat-cache, file-entry-cache, cacheable-request and the @cacheable scope taken alongside. Two details have no counterpart anywhere in yesterday's report. The first is that the malicious files went to each project's main branch before a release was tagged, so the compromised versions carry valid provenance signatures — the artefact a supply-chain auditor checks in order to conclude a package is clean now certifies the compromise instead. The second is a delivery path aimed at agent users specifically: the poisoned repository also ships a .claude/settings.json carrying a session-start hook and a .vscode/tasks.json task set to fire when the folder opens, both pointing at the same setup script, so opening the project in an editor or an agent executes it with no install involved at all. Set that against yesterday's Perception item, which made a point of staging autonomy — reversible actions first, starting with isolating a machine. Today's worm stages nothing. It sweeps npm tokens, GitHub credentials of every flavour including short-lived OIDC tokens, AWS and instance-metadata keys, Kubernetes service-account tokens, Vault, Stripe and Slack keys, SSH keys, Docker configs and Terraform state, then republishes itself through any publish token it finds, which is why researchers watched it move between organisations every two to seven minutes. Releases tied to Deliveroo, Qlik and Picsart were caught in the spread. The timing is its own note: the same report has Black Hat's AI Summit running today on agentic risk and a first-ever BSides Las Vegas track on prompt injection and software supply chains, both convening in Las Vegas while this was moving.

items.headline: Swiftlet runs an 80-billion-parameter Qwen on an M5 Mac in 4.3 gigabytes by streaming its experts off the disk
items.diff_narrative: Yesterday's model item and today's rest on the same architectural fact and point it in opposite directions. Yesterday Alibaba took Qwen3.8-Max generally available at 2.4 trillion total parameters with roughly 95 billion active per token — a sparse mixture-of-experts layout paired with hybrid attention — and sold it by the token at two dollars per million in and six per million out, the sparsity being the argument for why a model that size can be served at all. Today a Swift and Metal runtime called Swiftlet uses the same sparsity to argue the model need not be resident at all: Qwen3-Next-80B, 42 gigabytes of weights on disk, generating at 4.5 to 5 tokens a second on an M5 Mac while peaking at 4.3 gigabytes of resident memory, with a 35-billion-parameter Qwen3.6 at 2.6 gigabytes and 7 to 11 tokens a second, and the same model on an iPhone 17 in about 2.5 gigabytes at roughly one token a second. The family recurs but the artefact does not: Qwen3-Next-80B and Qwen3.6 are already-published weights this runtime consumes, not the Qwen3.8 line whose open weights Alibaba said yesterday it would release next week. What is genuinely new against yesterday is the method and the location of the ceiling. Attention, embeddings and routers stay permanently resident at four bits; the routed experts are packed into fixed-stride containers each retrievable in a single read and streamed as the router asks for them, with a cache the user sizes by flag holding the recent and frequent ones, and Gated DeltaNet linear attention across three-quarters of the layers stopping the key-value cache from eating the savings back. Cache hit rates run between 43 and 70 percent depending on how much memory is handed over, but throughput barely moves as that budget changes, because the bottleneck currently sits in GPU dispatch rather than in reading from storage — which says the streaming approach still has headroom, and recasts the memory ceiling on a laptop or a phone as a scheduling problem rather than a capacity one. One line connects it straight back to yesterday. Yesterday's Infinity item was a founder's account of coding agents writing a CUDA-equivalent stack for d-Matrix silicon in about ten hours, and the bullet itself flagged the claim as early and self-interested. Today's artefact is also agent-written — eight commits, Apache 2.0 — but it is a public repository with numbers anyone can clone and re-measure rather than an account of one, which is a different class of evidence for a closely related claim.

items.headline: Unsloth's largest merge in some time takes Studio into image and video generation and adds LoRA training for image models, with no package release attached
items.diff_narrative: This is the only subject carried directly from yesterday, and it inverts where the day's work is visible. Yesterday the change sat on the package index and not in the code: 2026.8.2 went to PyPI on Monday, August 3 with unsloth-zoo moving to the matching version the same day, and the bullet noted that the only commits on the main branch that day were a merge and a changelog edit. Today the change sits entirely in the repository and not on the package index. A pull request against the desktop Studio adds an Images page — text-to-image running on Unsloth's own GGUF quantisations of Z-Image, Qwen-Image, FLUX and SDXL variants, editing workflows covering transform, inpaint, extend, upscale and instruction-driven edits, text-to-video across five model families with synchronised audio, and QLoRA training for image models with live metrics and one-click deployment of the resulting adapter — at 79,151 lines added across 231 files, carrying more than eight hundred backend unit tests and browser-level end-to-end checks. Two inference paths sit underneath, native stable-diffusion.cpp and Diffusers, sharing GPU memory with the chat backend rather than competing with it for allocation, with batched image rendering measured at ten to twenty-two times faster than rendering the same images serially. Twenty-eight further commits went in the same day: Intel Arc detection and an XPU PyTorch install path in the Windows installer, with Arc, Iris, UHD and HD graphics now recognised and the wheels bundling their own oneAPI runtime so no separate Intel toolkit install is required, plus a run of release-pipeline hardening — signed installer plugin libraries with the release failing on any unsigned file, the WebView2 bootstrapper embedded rather than fetched, Defender scanning of Windows bundles before publication, and macOS disk-image stapling retried on failure. None of it shipped as a version. The published library still stands at yesterday's 2026.8.2, and today's bullet reports the documentation changelog still sitting at July 29, so a reader tracking this project by its package index sees nothing today at all. The subject moved too, and further than the merge size alone suggests. Yesterday's increment was about whether the weights arrive: an automatic fallback from XET to plain HTTP when XET stalls, and much lower memory during a transfer, framed by the team as making a large pull finish instead of hanging. Today's work is not about text weights in any form — it is a desktop application generating images and video and training adapters for image models. Two consecutive reports on the same project, the first about transport and the second about a modality the project had not shipped in, and the second of them arriving with the version number unchanged.

items.headline: HP, Asus and Acer put CXMT DRAM into non-US laptops because there is not enough of anyone else's
items.diff_narrative: Memory appeared in yesterday's report exactly once, and not as a story: a single clause inside the conference calendar describing FMS as the place the memory squeeze gets discussed by the people causing it. Today the squeeze is a lead item, and it lands on the morning FMS opens its twentieth edition in Santa Clara — the one room where the people causing the shortage and the people absorbing it are both present. Nikkei Asia reports HP, Asus and Acer shipping small volumes of DRAM from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies in notebooks sold outside the United States, qualification of the parts having completed around the middle of this year. The quantities are limited and the placement is deliberate — budget models, non-US markets — with Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron kept for regions where the regulatory and geopolitical exposure is higher, and HP described as still evaluating the supplier rather than committed to it. The reason is what makes it a change in the report rather than a procurement note. This is not a price move; ChangXin is not undercutting the incumbents. It is a supply move, taken in a market that the AI build-out has left tight enough that PC makers will qualify a supplier they had previously left alone. Read against yesterday's hardware item the two days sit at opposite layers of the same scarcity. Yesterday the scarce thing was software — an accelerator with no CUDA-equivalent stack, and a claim that coding agents can now write one in about ten hours, which is a bottleneck being argued away. Today the scarce thing is a commodity part with no software question attached, and it is not being argued away: a component notebook vendors used to treat as fungible now decides whether a machine ships at all. Today's other memory item runs the other direction and should not be folded into this one — Swiftlet reduces how much memory a model needs at runtime, not how much silicon a vendor can buy — but the report carries both on the same morning.

items.headline: Palantir prints 93 percent growth and reprices about 20 percent at the open, with AMD the next test after today's close
items.diff_narrative: Yesterday's report priced this sector once, and privately: Horizon3's 250 million dollar Series E above a two-billion valuation, roughly triple the 650 million it carried out of its Series D in June 2025, on operating numbers of approaching 100 million dollars in annual recurring revenue growing 120 percent year over year. A valuation set by an oversubscribed round is a figure a small group agreed on with no daily mark against it. Today the same question is answered on a public tape in a single session, and two orders of magnitude up. Palantir reported second-quarter revenue of 1.94 billion dollars after Monday's close, up 93 percent year over year against a 1.81 billion consensus, with adjusted earnings of 41 cents against 34 expected, net income of 1.06 billion and adjusted free cash flow of 1.22 billion. The split underneath has no equivalent anywhere in yesterday's text: United States commercial revenue rose 149 percent to 764 million dollars against United States government revenue up 90 percent to 809 million, which leaves the commercial side nearly the size of the government business the company was long assumed to depend on. Guidance moved with it — full year to between 8.15 and 8.16 billion dollars from a prior 7.65 to 7.66, the United States commercial target lifted above 3.42 billion implying at least 134 percent growth, and the third quarter guided to roughly 2.16 billion. Shares opened this morning around 152 dollars against Monday's 125.65 close. Analysts moved in one direction and by very different amounts: Deutsche Bank upgraded to Buy and took its target from 80 dollars to 200, Citi went to 245 from 200, DA Davidson to 200 from 175. What makes this a change in the report rather than a ticker note is the question it settles, which yesterday's items only circled. Yesterday's round priced a thesis about automated security; today's print answers the broader one the sector has been working around — whether enterprise AI software spend is converting into recognised revenue at scale rather than into pilots — and answers it unambiguously for at least one vendor. Unlike anything yesterday carried, today's item also names its own next test: AMD reports after the close today, which puts the same question to the silicon side, with the data-centre line and any quantified Helios rack-scale orders the specific things to read.

items.headline: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events: four entries close, Black Hat reaches Summit Day, Ai4 and FMS both open, and a first BSides AI-security track appears
items.diff_narrative: The calendar moved at both ends and should not be read as carried forward. Four things have closed since yesterday. Ai4's pre-conference programme, which yesterday opened at The Venetian, is over. AI Tinkerers Columbus, which ran yesterday from 5:30 to 8 PM EDT, has passed; that chapter's next date is Monday, September 7. IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026's workshop, tutorial and competition proposal deadline closed yesterday anywhere on Earth, and with it the last submission window that conference had open — the paper deadline went on July 27 and supplementary video on July 30 — so all that entry now carries is a decision calendar running from competition decisions on September 21 to camera-ready papers on October 26. And DEF CON's pricing collapses to a single number: yesterday carried both the 600 dollar late pre-registration tier that had closed on Friday, July 31 and the 520 dollar cash door, with the observation that the door had become the cheaper way in; today the tier is gone from the text and the door is simply what remains. Four things started. Black Hat reaches its Summit Day today at the Mandalay Bay Convention Center, and it arrives with detail yesterday did not have: six summits running in parallel — Healthcare, CISO, AI, Financial Threat, Innovators and Investors, and the Omdia Analyst Summit — with the AI Summit in its third year covering securing AI systems, agentic risk, cloud and GPU infrastructure protection and the use of AI in both offence and defence, worth five continuing-education credits to certified attendees. Trainings, listed yesterday as running through today, close today. Ai4's main conference opened this morning and gained four keynote themes, twenty industry and technical tracks, and Dmitri Dolgov of Waymo and Sebastian Thrun beside the Hinton, Fei-Fei Li and Ng billing already carried. FMS opened its twentieth edition today and went from one clause about the memory squeeze to a sized event: more than 350 speakers, over 100 exhibitors, twenty-plus content streams and 3,500 attendees expected from 1,500 organisations. Two AI Tinkerers sessions listed yesterday for tomorrow — Paris with Paris.rb, now described as a session on coding with AI, and the Seattle dev-tools track — run today. One entry is entirely new and was already live when it appeared: BSides Las Vegas is running its first dedicated AI-security track, [un]prompted, built with the standalone conference of the same name, on prompt injection, agentic systems, GitHub exploits, software supply chains and defensive engineering, pitched at practitioners on the assumption that the systems under discussion already hold credentials and autonomy. It opened yesterday on a three-day schedule and closes tomorrow, so it was running while yesterday's calendar did not carry it. Elsewhere the movement is small and mostly framing. The AI Risk Summit's Friday, August 7 step from 1,895 to 2,195 dollars is now flagged as the nearest money deadline on the list. Palo Alto on Tuesday, August 18 stays unverified, with the reason lengthening from a refusal recorded yesterday to a chapter page that has been refusing requests for days, and still no entry on the global calendar. The Zenity contradiction is unchanged and still unresolved: the call-for-speakers page lists no Asia edition while the company's own events page describes an undated Asia expansion, and the third-party Tokyo-in-September report remains uncorroborated at source. Two small details dropped rather than moved — AI Village's room is still W603 on Level 1 but the venue name no longer travels with it, and Bedrock's Vincent Gonguet loses the newly-listed marker that introduced him yesterday. The silicon bullet stands exactly as carried, word for word: Hot Chips from Sunday, August 23 to Tuesday, August 25 with its tutorial and session lists, then the run from the AI Infra Summit in September through GTC Berlin to SC26. So do the remaining San Francisco and autumn entries — the end-of-September collision, the AI Security Summit and the AI Engineering and Infrastructure Summit both landing on Thursday, October 15, SANS and OWASP in November, and the ACM workshop in The Hague.
